title: Which way does the equilibrium lie
asks: An acid and a base are mixed. Say which side is favoured, estimate K, or choose a base strong enough to do the job.

know.h: Every proton transfer has an acid on each side: the species that gives the proton on the left, and the species that would give it back on the right. Be able to find both.
The equilibrium favours the weaker acid (the higher {{pKa}}), which always sits with the weaker base. The stronger acid and stronger base are the pair that react.

Lecture examples: {{H2O}} (15.7) + {{HO-}} gives {{HO-}} + {{H2O}} (15.7), K = 1. {{H2O}} (15.7) + {{NH2-}} gives {{HO-}} + {{NH3}} (38), to the right. {{NH3}} (38) + {{CH3-}} gives {{NH2-}} + {{CH4}} (50 to 60), to the right.
K as a power of ten: {{pKa}} = -log {{Ka}}, so K = 10x with x = {{pKa}} of the acid on the product side minus {{pKa}} of the acid on the reactant side. A positive x favours products.

Numbers to have ready: H-I -10, H-Br -9, H-Cl -8, {{H3O+}} -1.5, {{RCO2H}} 4, H-F 4, {{H2S}} 10, phenol 10, {{RNH3+}} about 10.5, water 15.7, alcohols 16 (tert-butanol 17), terminal alkyne 25, {{NH3}} 38, alkane 50 to 60.

Is this base strong enough? A base deprotonates an acid essentially completely when the base's conjugate acid has a {{pKa}} several units above that of the acid. Be able to write the conjugate acid of any base.
Common bases by the {{pKa}} of their conjugate acids: acetate 4; {{HS-}} 10; {{HO-}} 15.7; {{CH3O-}} and {{CH3CH2O-}} about 16; {{(CH3)3CO-}} 17; acetylide 25; {{NH2-}} 38; R-Li and R-MgX 50 to 60.
Use the value of the species as drawn. An ammonium ion {{RNH3+}} is about 10.5, a neutral amine N-H is 38. {{H3O+}} is -1.5, water is 15.7.
Organolithium (R-Li) and Grignard (R-MgX) reagents act as R:-: the carbon carries the electron density, and they are very strong bases.

Water destroys them: {{CH3Li}} + {{H2O}} gives {{CH4}} + LiOH. The carbon lone pair takes H from water and the H-O electrons go to oxygen. Water is about 15.7 and methane 50 to 60, so K is 1034 or more.
So they are made without any O-H: R-Li from R-Br and 2 Li in pentane, R-MgX from R-X and Mg in diethyl ether. Any O-H, N-H, S-H or terminal alkyne C-H protonates them.
{{D2O}} puts D where the metal was: 2-bromopropane, then Mg in ether, then {{D2O}}, gives propane with D on the middle carbon. {{H2O}} gives plain propane.

method: Find the proton that moves, and mark the acid on the left and the acid on the right.
Write the {{pKa}} of each of those two acids, for the species exactly as drawn (mind charges).
The side with the higher {{pKa}} is favoured. If the two values are equal, K = 1.
For K, subtract: {{pKa}} of the product-side acid minus {{pKa}} of the reactant-side acid is the exponent. Check that its sign agrees with the previous step.
To choose a base, write the conjugate acid of each candidate and keep those whose {{pKa}} is above that of the acid to be deprotonated.
If R-Li or R-MgX is present, treat it as a carbanion and look for any hydrogen more acidic than an alkane: it will be removed first.

pitfalls.h: Favouring the side with the stronger acid. The equilibrium collects the weaker acid and the weaker base.
Subtracting the wrong way round and getting the sign of the exponent wrong. Check it against which side holds the weaker acid.
Using 38 for an ammonium ion or 11 for a neutral amine. Match the number to the charge that is drawn.
Assuming hydroxide or an alkoxide can deprotonate anything. They cannot remove a terminal alkyne hydrogen (25) or an amine N-H (38).
Treating a Grignard or organolithium reagent as stable to water or alcohols, or putting the acid workup in the same step as the reagent.
Comparing an acid with a base directly. Always compare two acids: the acid, and the conjugate acid of the base.
